fatal_errors: The proposed carbon-addition/TiC intervention does not reconstruct the target intervention of high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering.

It assumes an equimolar single-phase FCC starting structure, whereas the target mechanism centers on a nonequilibrium nanocrystalline FCC/BCC structure, lattice strain, and milling-induced dislocation accumulation.
The falsification rule treats failure to form TiC as falsification of the strengthening mechanism, although that would instead mean the intervention was not successfully implemented.
TiC precipitation and local chemical ordering are bundled as interchangeable interventions, preventing attribution of any strength change to one defined mediator.
explanation: The hypothesis directly addresses the hardness–plasticity tradeoff and offers a testable dislocation-obstacle explanation. Its controlled baseline-versus-carbon-added comparison and TEM/EDS plus mechanical testing could support a plausible alternative precipitation-strengthening study. The cited evidence supports TiC-associated second-phase strengthening in related CoCrFeNiTix alloys, but it does not establish that controlled carbon addition governs the low strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi. Relative to the hidden target, the central processing route, quantitative conditions, nanocrystalline grain-boundary strengthening, milling-induced strain/dislocation density, FCC/BCC phase fractions, densification, and quantitative hardness and compressive-strength outcomes are absent. The proposed comparison also changes composition and potentially phase constitution, so it is not a clean test of why the nominal simple-solid-solution starting state is weak. A stronger falsification design would first verify comparable density and successful TiC formation, then correlate precipitate size and volume fraction with strength while controlling grain size, phase fraction, and interstitial solid-solution effects.
